problems.title: Order changes the answer
hints: The spacing of FP32 numbers near 10⁸ is 8.
problems.solution: (a) 0: 10⁸ + 1 rounds back to 10⁸. (b) 1. Parallel sums choose an order; different orders give different bits.

problems.title: ULPs
problems.solution: (a) $2^{-23} ≈ 1.19 \times 10^{-7}$. (b) 10⁶ is between $2^{19}$ and $2^{20}$: ULP $2^{-4} = 0.0625$. Compare results in ULPs or relative error, never with a fixed absolute tolerance.

problems.title: Determinism checklist
problems.statement: Which make a reduction's result bit-identical across runs on the same GPU?

options: A fixed reduction tree with the same launch shape
Per-block partials summed in index order
Changing the grid size between runs

problems.solution: Fixed trees and fixed-order partial sums are deterministic; atomics and changing launch shapes aren't.

problems.title: Kahan in numbers

parts.prompt: Exact sum of the FP32 values?

hints: Simulate it, or reason about the growing ULP.
problems.solution: Plain: 9998.56; Kahan: 10000.00; exact 10000.0001 (FP32's 0.1 is slightly above 0.1). The plain sum's error grows with n; Kahan's stays at a few ULPs.

problems.title: Tolerances for tests
problems.statement: A GPU GEMM (K = 4096, FP32, inputs ~ U(−1, 1)) is compared with a CPU FP64 reference.

options: Relative error bound scaled by √K or K times FP32 epsilon, or exact inputs (Lab 4)

problems.solution: A tolerance derived from the reduction length and unit roundoff, or inputs designed so all arithmetic is exact. Fixed tiny absolute tolerances fail randomly; huge ones hide bugs.

problems.title: FP16 overflow

parts.prompt: A dot product of length 4,096 of values around 8, accumulated in FP16…

problems.solution: 262,144 overflows FP16 to inf. Accumulate in FP32; scale inputs if they're large.

problems.title: Deterministic algorithms in frameworks

options: Selects kernels without float atomics where possible
Raises an error for operations with no deterministic implementation
Makes results identical across different GPU models

problems.solution: It picks deterministic kernels, errors where none exist, and costs some speed. It doesn't promise identical bits across GPUs or library versions.

problems.title: Pairwise error growth
problems.statement: Worst-case error bounds for summing n numbers in floating point: sequential ≈ (n − 1)u·Σ|x|, pairwise ≈ ⌈log₂ n⌉u·Σ|x|.

parts.prompt: Ratio of the bounds for n = 2²⁰?

problems.solution: About 52,429×. GPU tree reductions are, as a side effect, far more accurate than a CPU loop: "the GPU's sum disagrees with the CPU" often means the CPU is the less accurate one.

problems.title: Fused multiply-add
problems.statement: Comparing a GPU result with a CPU result of a*b + c.

parts.prompt: Why might they differ in the last bit?
options: The GPU compiler contracted to an FMA (one rounding) where the CPU used two roundings

problems.solution: FMA contraction (default in nvcc). Disable with -fmad=false to compare, but the FMA result is usually the more accurate one.

problems.title: Reproducing across runs
problems.statement: A training run's loss curves differ slightly between two identical launches.

options: Atomics in a reduction or embedding backward

problems.solution: Atomic accumulation order, algorithm selection by autotuners, and RNG. Clock speed changes timing, which changes atomic order, but isn't itself a numerical input.
